title: FIERY SERPENTS ENTERED ISRAEL’S CAMP—THEN GOD TOLD MOSES TO RAISE A BRONZE SERPENT
paragraphs: FIERY SERPENTS ENTERED ISRAEL’S CAMP—THEN GOD TOLD MOSES TO RAISE A BRONZE SERPENT
They were dying from the bite. God did not tell them to pretend the venom wasn't there. He told them to look at something lifted up—and centuries later, Jesus said their story was pointing to Him.
Imagine hearing the screaming before you understand what is happening.
Someone tears open a tent flap.
Another person falls into the sand.
And suddenly the camp realizes something terrifying is moving among them.

Israel had survived Egypt. They had watched the Red Sea open. They had eaten bread that appeared with the morning dew. They had seen water come from a rock. They had witnessed a mountain tremble beneath the presence of God.
That is what makes Numbers 21 so uncomfortable.
Because the people in this story are not people who had never seen God move.
They are people who had seen Him move repeatedly...
and still allowed unbelief to poison their hearts.
Maybe that is why this story feels frighteningly close to home.
You can have answered prayers in your history and complaints in your mouth today.
You can remember what God delivered you from and still resent where He is leading you.
You can know Scripture and still struggle to trust the Author.
You can sing on Sunday and privately ask on Monday,
“God, why have You brought me here?”
Israel was traveling around Edom, and Numbers tells us that “the soul of the people was much discouraged because of the way.”
They spoke against God and Moses.
Why had they been brought out of Egypt?
Why were they in the wilderness?
Why was there no ordinary food and water?
Why did they despise the provision God had given them?
“And the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people, and they bit the people; and much people of Israel died.”
Literally, “the serpents, the burning ones” or “fiery serpents.”
The word connected with “serpent” is נָחָשׁ — nāḥāš.
The word translated “fiery” comes from שָׂרָף — śārāf, associated with burning.
Scripture does not explicitly tell us whether “fiery” describes their appearance, their venom's burning effect, or another characteristic. We should not pretend to know what God has not revealed.
What Scripture does reveal is enough.
Funny how quickly the things we thought were unbearable can become small when we finally see the condition of our souls.
There are three words pride hates saying:
Yet those words can become the doorway through which repentance begins.
Some of us have spent years renaming what God has already named.
We call unforgiveness “having boundaries,” even when the boundary has quietly become hatred.
And sometimes we spend so much energy explaining our wounds that we never confess the ways we have wounded others.
Then God gave him one of the strangest instructions in the Old Testament.
Anyone who has been bitten may look at it and live.
So Moses made a serpent of bronze.
The similarity between the Hebrew sounds for serpent and bronze makes the expression memorable.
But think about how strange the command must have sounded.
The people had been bitten by serpents...
and God told Moses to raise the likeness of a serpent before them.
You are lying in the dust.
And perhaps everything inside you wants something more complicated.
Surely there must be something I can do.
But the dying Israelite did not need to understand every mystery surrounding the bronze serpent.
He needed to trust the word God had spoken.
And this is where the story becomes much bigger than Numbers 21.
Because centuries later, Jesus Christ reached back into Israel's wilderness and told us where the deepest meaning of that lifted serpent was ultimately pointing.
A man with knowledge, reputation, theology, and questions.
And Jesus told him that he needed something he could never accomplish through religious credentials.
He needed to be born again.
Καὶ καθὼς Μωϋσῆς ὕψωσεν τὸν ὄφιν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ...
Kai kathōs Mōysēs hypsōsen ton ophin en tē erēmō...
“And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness...”
Then came the words that transform the wilderness story:
“...even so must the Son of man be lifted up.”
The Greek verb ὑψόω — hypsoō — means to lift up or raise up.
But we must be careful here.
Jesus is not saying that He is evil.
He is not saying the serpent was secretly divine.
He is not telling us to worship the bronze object.
The comparison centers upon the God-appointed lifting up and the life received by those who believe.
The Israelites were dying and could not save themselves.
Humanity is dying in sin and cannot save itself.
The dying person looked in faith.
And Jesus declares that the Son of Man would likewise be lifted up so that whoever believes in Him may have eternal life.
Now the wilderness becomes a mirror.
Because the serpent's venom was killing bodies.
Sin is killing something far deeper.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
The person reading Christian articles while secretly drifting from Christ.
The person everybody thinks is strong.
The person who knows exactly how to raise their hands during worship while carrying a private life they desperately hope nobody discovers.
The Gospel begins where our excuses end.
Christianity is not the announcement that bad people should try harder to become respectable.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners who cannot rescue themselves have been offered salvation through Jesus Christ.
The eternal Son of God took upon Himself true humanity.
And the One who knew no sin bore our sin.
The cross exposes something devastating about us:
Our condition was so serious that moral improvement could never cure it.
But the cross reveals something breathtaking about God:
His love was so great that He gave His Son to save sinners.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
The scandal is that creatures made by God rebel against their Creator and then convince themselves that we are basically fine.
The scandal is that humanity crucified the sinless Son of God.
Grace is that the cross where humanity displayed its rebellion became the place where Christ accomplished redemption.
Grace is Jesus praying for His enemies.
Grace is blood shed for sinners.
Grace is forgiveness offered to the guilty.
Grace is the condemned thief hearing hope while dying beside the King.
Grace is Peter being restored after denying Jesus.
Grace is Saul the persecutor becoming Paul the apostle.
Grace is God taking people whose stories should have ended in judgment and giving them a new ending through Christ.
But there is another warning hidden inside the bronze-serpent story that many people never mention.
And eventually something God had once used became something Israel worshiped.
During the reign of Hezekiah, Scripture says the Israelites were burning incense to that bronze serpent.
Something once associated with God's deliverance had become an idol.
And that should frighten every religious heart.
Because we can begin worshiping what God used instead of worshiping God.
A ministry can become an idol.
A pastor can become an idol.
A church tradition can become an idol.
A worship style can become an idol.
A theological tribe can become an idol.
A Christian page can become an idol.
Even memories of yesterday's encounter with God can become substitutes for walking with God today.
The bronze serpent could not save anyone independently of God's word.
And eventually, when people treated it like an object of worship, it had to be smashed.
If Gospel Warrior ever helps you, let it help you look beyond Gospel Warrior toward Christ.
If an article convicts you, do not worship the messenger.
If a devotional strengthens you, do not merely admire the devotional.
Because the purpose of Christian ministry is not to gather spectators around a bronze object.
It is to point dying people toward the living Christ.
Maybe you have been bitten by things nobody sees.
A wound you turned into permission to wound others.
A private addiction beneath a public smile.
Sin that once disturbed you now feels normal.
but somewhere inside, you know something is dying.
You do not need to clean yourself up enough to become worthy of looking to Jesus.
Look to Jesus because you are not worthy—and because He is merciful.
Repentance does not mean pretending you never sinned.
Repentance means turning from sin toward the Savior.
Faith is not pretending the venom is harmless.
Maybe you think you have gone too far.
Maybe you failed again last night.
Maybe everyone thinks you are spiritually healthy while you know you are barely breathing.
Maybe shame whispers that Jesus wants everyone except you.
Not to your promises that “this time I'll do better.”
The serpent was raised in a wilderness full of dying people.
Jesus was raised on a cross for a world full of sinners.
And unlike the bronze serpent, Jesus did not remain an object hanging on a pole.
The grave did not write the final sentence.
That is why your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
There is reconciliation with God in Christ.
There is a new heart in Christ.
There is power to fight sin in Christ.
There is resurrection hope in Christ.
There is grace for repentant sinners in Christ.
And maybe right now your greatest need is not another inspirational quote.
Maybe you need to stop hiding.
Call it what He calls it.
And where your sin has harmed someone, seek biblical reconciliation and make things right where possible.
You may have spent years trying to manage venom.
If you genuinely need His mercy, comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to remember you in prayer, simply comment, “pray for me.”
And if Christ has already pulled you from a place you thought would destroy you, tell your testimony. Someone reading the comments may be standing where you once stood.
Do not turn vulnerability into theater.
That share could become an invitation to open Scripture.

If you want to glorify God through supporting Gospel work, don't let that support become empty religious consumerism. Worship belongs to God alone. But generosity, sharing biblical truth, encouraging Gospel ministry, and helping others encounter Scripture can be genuine acts of Christian stewardship when they flow from love for Christ rather than pressure or self-glory.
The gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because sometimes confession, testimony, encouragement, and prayer begin when one believer finally stops pretending.
Then close Facebook for a moment.
And when you reach the words about Moses lifting up the serpent in the wilderness, remember:
Jesus knew exactly where humanity's story was going.
The Israelites looked upward because death was already working inside them.
Perhaps that is the image you need to carry with you tonight.
Not people pretending they were never bitten.
Not people boasting about how little venom they had.
Dying people looking toward the provision God had given.
And now Christ calls sinners to something greater.
Your sin may explain how you reached this wilderness.
Your scars may testify to battles you wish you had never fought.
Your consequences may not disappear overnight.
But for the person who turns to Jesus Christ in repentant faith, sin does not get the final word.
Shame does not get the final word.
Your addiction does not get the final word.
Your past does not get the final word.
The grave does not get the final word.
The venom may explain why you fell—but the cross announces why your story does not have to end in the dust.
